I am 72 years old. My back is not what it used to be, and my son works in a factory in the county town, so it is mostly me, my wife, and occasional help from my daughter-in-law in the fields. I have farmed this land for 50 years, and I know every corner of my 9 mu. I do not need books to tell me what works.

This year, I will keep 6 mu in my wheat-maize rotation. That system has fed my family for decades. The other 3 mu I will plant with cotton. Cotton is hard work, especially at harvest, but it gives me cash in hand, and I need cash for medicine and for my grandson’s school.

For the winter wheat, I will sow in early October on 6 mu. I will use an improved variety I have been planting for years—I have saved seed from the last good harvest, and I know it stands well against the cold winds here in Quzhou. Before sowing, I will run the rotary tiller to break the stubble from last summer’s maize. I will put down compound fertilizer as a base and then topdress urea at the jointing stage. I will irrigate three times from my well: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the frost, once at jointing in spring, and once at grain filling. Two sprays should be enough—one herbicide after sowing and one insecticide if the aphids come.

For summer maize, time is short after the wheat harvest in June. I will plant hybrid seed directly into the wheat stubble without ploughing. There is no time to waste, and the no-till machines work fine. Maize needs nitrogen, but I know 14 kg per mu is enough if I apply it at the right time. I will irrigate twice if the summer rains are light—once at the big flare stage and once at filling. Two pesticide applications: one for weeds and one if the corn borer appears.

For cotton on the remaining 3 mu, I will plough deeply in April because cotton roots need soft, deep soil. I will plant hybrid Bt cotton seed to cut down on bollworm sprays. Cotton is thirsty, so I will irrigate three times during the peak flowering and boll periods. I will fertilize with 12 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. Three pesticide sprays should do—cotton always needs more watching than grain.

I do not chase record yields anymore. At my age, I want stability, not surprises. I use what I know, I do not waste inputs, and I let the land do what it has always done.
